definition: Liquidity describes how easy it is to find a trading counterparty and how cheap it is to trade; a liquid market/asset has ready counterparties and low trading cost, while an illiquid market/asset is hard to trade and relatively costly to transact in.
core_idea: Difficulty finding trading partners is a distinct complication in energy markets, and the ease or cost of finding a counterparty is what traders mean by liquidity.
key_points: A liquid asset (e.g., a U.S. government bond) can be bought or sold on short notice.
An illiquid asset (e.g., a nuclear power plant) may have real value but be hard to sell quickly at a fair price.
The most liquid parts of the energy market are the forward financial markets, in contrast to the more complicated spot markets.
relationships: Ties to the spot-vs-forward market split: spot markets tend to be less liquid/more locally constrained than forward financial markets.
trading_implications: Traders should expect higher transaction costs and more difficulty exiting positions in illiquid energy markets/assets compared to liquid ones.
